scores.rationale: None of the snippets directly addresses the stylized fact that cells in a tissue are metabolically similar regardless of organism size. Most snippets concern allometric scaling of metabolic rate with organism mass, cell/organelle size control, genome size, or cytoskeletal mechanics—topically adjacent but not evidentiary for cellular metabolic invariance across organism sizes. Snippet 3 weakly touches the notion that somatic cells share genetic makeup, which is tangentially relevant but does not address metabolic similarity. Several snippets emphasize that cell size and metabolic activity covary with genome and body size (7, 8, 14), which could even complicate the claim, but none make the specific tissue-level metabolic comparison across organism sizes. Overall the corpus provides no clear support and no clear contradiction, so evidence is weak and the direction is best judged neutral/insufficient.

snippets.text: According to the "cell theory" in its original form, morphogenesis in multicellular organisms results from oriented cell divisions and cell growth. This view is based on the still-valid fact that cells represent the smallest structural and functional units exhibiting all fundamental properties and manifestations of life. Each cell stores, replicates, and partially expresses the genetic information of an organism.

snippets.title: Interspecific allometric scaling of unicellular organisms as an evolutionary process of food chain creation
snippets.label: neutral
snippets.text: Metabolism of living organisms is a foundation of life. The metabolic rate (energy production per unit time) increases slower than organisms' mass. When this phenomenon is considered across different species, it is called interspecific allometric scaling, whose causes are unknown. We argue that the cause of interspecific allometric scaling is the total effect of physiological and adaptation mechanisms inherent to organisms composing a food chain.

Most animal cells are 10-50 microns in diameter, whereas the macromolecules that comprise them are 10,000-fold smaller (2-20 nm). To establish long-range order over cellular length scales, individual molecules must, therefore, self-assemble into larger polymers, with lengths (0.1-20 m) comparable to the size of a cell. These polymers must then be cross-linked into organized networks that fill the cytoplasm.

snippets.title: Go with the flow – bulk transport by molecular motors
snippets.label: neutral
snippets.text: ABSTRACT Cells are the smallest building blocks of all living eukaryotic organisms, usually ranging from a couple of micrometers (for example, platelets) to hundreds of micrometers (for example, neurons and oocytes) in size. In eukaryotic cells that are more than 100 µm in diameter, very often a self-organized large-scale movement of cytoplasmic contents, known as cytoplasmic streaming, occurs to compensate for the physical constraints of large cells.
